rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to measure how the crowded early cluster responds to slope. This will distinguish slope-sensitive overlaps from pairs that need a temperature or starting-composition adjustment.
The shallower gradient improved the early cluster but incurred a time penalty. Test higher temperature at the original slope to shift selectivity within that cluster while shortening retention.
At 60 C only one pair remains below baseline resolution. Test a shallower gradient to improve that pair, using the available retention-time margin below 10 minutes.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a steeper gradient instead. This should shorten the run and reveal whether that pair can improve without compromising its neighboring separation.

Test intermediate temperature to map selectivity in the early three-peak cluster, since changing slope alone has not resolved it. Keeping the original gradient isolates temperature effects and should keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction to change selectivity in the remaining overlap, which slope adjustments alone have not resolved. Retain a moderate gradient duration to protect the neighboring pair while keeping the run comfortably below 10 minutes.
Injection 7 reached the maximum CRF, so shorten its gradient by one grid step to test whether full resolution can be retained in less time. Keep injection 7 as the fully resolved fallback.

Narrow the gradient window to give a slope between injections 7 and 8, aiming to restore both marginal pairs above R = 1.5 while eluting faster than injection 7. The lower endpoint remains above the estimated organic fraction at which the last peak eluted.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction can shorten retention while preserving full resolution; the slightly narrower window also makes the gradient shallower. Monitor the early cluster for compression, retaining injection 9 as the faster fully resolved reference.

With maximum CRF already secured, explore the low-temperature selectivity regime for an alternative fully resolved, fast method. The steep, broad gradient should limit late retention while testing whether the crowded cluster separates in a different elution order.

Return to the successful high-temperature window and modestly reduce the slope to increase the critical-pair resolution margin. The endpoint remains above the last peak’s estimated elution composition, so full elution below 10 minutes is expected.

Test one temperature step below the fastest fully resolved method to measure local temperature sensitivity of the critical cluster. This will establish whether nearby selectivity offers another optimization direction or whether 60 C is essential.

Test a slope just steeper than injection 9 to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary more closely. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, while the critical pair is expected to be near R = 1.5.

Test a shallower gradient at the higher starting fraction to restore the compressed early pair seen in injection 10. This may provide another fully resolved window; injection 14 is not fully resolved despite its rounded CRF of 1.000.

Reduce the endpoint one grid step to make the gradient slightly shallower and lift injection 15’s remaining R = 1.47 pair above 1.5. The last peak should still elute near the gradient end and comfortably before 10 minutes.

Shift the successful injection 9 window downward while keeping its slope fixed to isolate starting-composition effects. This tests whether the intermediate starting fraction offers a better balance between the two critical early separations.
Back off one endpoint step from injection 14 to restore its marginal critical pair above R = 1.5. This should retain a six-minute programmed gradient with the last peak eluting near its end.

Test a shallower gradient in the successful 0.15–0.65 window to increase the critical-pair margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

With maximum CRF secured, test whether a shallower gradient increases the critical-pair margin while retaining a last-peak time below 10 minutes. Keep injection 9 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved option.

Preserve injection 9’s slope through the critical early cluster but end the programmed gradient sooner. This tests whether a shorter gradient can retain maximum CRF, although the last compounds will elute during the hold and may take longer.

Refine the higher-starting-composition branch with a slope between injections 15 and 16, targeting its R = 1.5 boundary. This may shorten retention relative to injection 16 while preserving maximum CRF; injection 9 remains the fastest fully resolved reference.

Test the endpoint one grid step above injection 9 to check the faster boundary directly. The critical pair may fall just below R = 1.5, in which case injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Back off to a slightly shallower slope than injection 9 to gain resolution margin with only a modest retention-time increase. This should provide a fully resolved compromise between injection 9’s speed and injection 12’s greater margin.

Preserve injection 12’s resolving slope but end the gradient earlier, testing a lower-organic endpoint expected to retain maximum CRF with the last peak still below 10 minutes. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
